big_idea: Smaller units = more units needed. Bigger units = fewer units. INVERSE relationship.
learning_intention: We are learning about the inverse relationship between unit size and count.
student_learning_goal: I can pick a non-standard unit and explain the inverse relationship.
success_criteria: I can pick the right UNIT for the object.
I can MEASURE with that unit.
I can explain why SMALLER units need MORE.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Roo and Cal — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Non-Standard Unit Set (60 cubes + 12 hand-span + 12 footprint per pair)

minds_on.hook: Roo: A pencil = 12 CUBES long! But only 2 HAND-SPANS! Smaller units = MORE. Bigger units = FEWER! Roo opens: 'SMALL unit, BIG count — BIG unit, small count!'

steps.instruction: Whole group: measure 2 objects with cubes AND hand-spans.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Same object, different unit. Different count?'

steps.instruction: Three stations. A: Cube measure 5 small objects. B: Hand-span measure 5 medium objects. C: Footstep measure 5 distances.
Stretch at C: measure same distance 3 ways and compare.
Discuss: smaller unit, bigger count. Inverse rule.
steps.teacher_prompt: Show: 24 cubes vs 4 hand-spans vs 1 footstep.

steps.instruction: PREDICT-THEN-MEASURE: Child PREDICTS the count for a hand-span before measuring, then compares with a partner who used cubes. Class shares whose count was closest. Cite Sarama & Clements (2009) — prediction sharpens unit-attribute matching.
steps.teacher_prompt: Roo: 'PREDICT first. Then MEASURE. Your prediction trains your sense.'

differentiation.for_movement_learners: Use feet directly to measure room size. NO-MATERIALS PATH: use HAND-SPAN, FOOTSTEP, FINGER-WIDTH directly on classroom objects — body becomes the ruler.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: picks unit; measures correctly; explains inverse.

discussion_prompts: Why do smaller units give bigger counts?
Roo's preview: tomorrow STANDARD units (cm, m) so EVERY classroom counts the same way (Lesson 2 — E2.1). Why might hand-spans not be enough?
consolidation.exit_routine: Roo's refrain — chant 3x: 'SMALL unit, BIG count — BIG unit, small count!' Each child records one object with two units.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 surfaces children with G1 unit experience.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child uses CUBES for EVERYTHING — repairing the wrong-tool trap at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On 'pick a non-standard unit and measure', the dominant Grade-2 trap is unit-choice / iteration confusion: child picks an unit without considering whether it FITS the attribute, or iterates with gaps. Sarama & Clements (2009) measurement learning trajectories and Lehrer (2003) place unit-iteration as the gateway to standard-unit work in Lesson 2.

Today: pick units, iterate without gaps. Tomorrow STANDARD units (cm, m) so EVERY classroom counts the same way (Lesson 2 — E2.1). Lesson 3 ruler use; Lesson 4 time; Lesson 5 capstone.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at Station C. Child trying to measure a 5-metre hallway with cubes. After 50 cubes still going.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You're at 50 cubes! Roo asks — how many MORE will it take?'

Guide. 'Big objects need BIG units. Use FOOTSTEPS instead. How many footsteps to the door?'

Child walks. 'About 10!'

'Right. 10 footsteps is FAST to measure. 200 cubes would take forever.'

Generlise. 'Roo says — pick the unit for the SIZE. Small = small unit. Big = big unit.'

If still using cubes for everything: provide 'unit-choice' chart matching object size to unit.
common_misconceptions: Cubes work for everything. (Repair: pick unit for SIZE.)
Smaller unit = more accurate always. (Repair: pick PRACTICAL unit.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child can name a unit but iterates with gaps: drill 'edge-to-edge, no spaces'; child re-measures using cubes as a model of contiguous iteration.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child picks a wrong-attribute unit (paper clip for area): name the attribute first ('we're measuring LENGTH'); child re-picks a length unit.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child can pick + iterate but loses count mid-row: chunk in fives ('5, 10, 15, ...') OR provide a tally row to mark each iteration.

parts_outline.task: Match 5 objects to the best unit (cubes/hand-spans/footsteps).
Measure a pencil with cubes AND hand-spans. Note the inverse.
Pick 3 home objects. Choose unit for each.
